extracted.intended_audience: researchers and clinicians developing, evaluating, or using clinical/observational measurement instruments (scale developers, psychometricians, health clinicians)
extracted.subtask_short: assessing reliability and validity of scales
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical standards for evaluating the reliability (inter- and intra-rater) and validity of clinical/observational measurement tools, including which statistics to report, study design elements (blinding, test-retest intervals), and interpretation of effect sizes. Applicable across clinical, rehabilitation, imaging, and observational audit instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement between different assessors rating the same subjects or items (e.g., two independent physiotherapists, two assessors on the same day).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify with percent agreement, Cohen's kappa (κ), weighted kappa (κw), or intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) depending on measure type; report specific values (examples: κ = 0.91, κ = 0.48, ICC = 0.77–1.00). Use standardized protocols and blinded raters to improve reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intra-rater (test–retest) reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Stability of the same rater's assessments over time (e.g., same assessor on different days or repeated sessions three weeks apart).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure with ICC, kappa, or test–retest reliability statistics; report time interval used (examples: 48 hours, 3 weeks). Include intrarater agreement statistics and confidence intervals (examples: weighted kappa = 0.83, ICC = 0.83).

rubrics_metrics.name: Percent agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Raw proportion of cases where raters give the same rating (e.g., 83% agreement between two physiotherapists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report as supplement to chance-corrected statistics; note that percent agreement does not account for agreement by chance and may overstate reliability for low-prevalence categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohen's kappa and weighted kappa
rubrics_metrics.description: Chance-corrected agreement measure for categorical ratings; weighted kappa for ordinal scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use weighted kappa for ordinal/graded categories (examples: κw = 0.48, κw = 0.36–0.85). Report confidence limits and interpret ranges (e.g., moderate, substantial, almost perfect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of reliability for continuous or interval data and for event/frame detection reproducibility (e.g., ICC2.1 for gait-event frame detection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify ICC model and form, report ICC with 95% CI, and accompany with SEM and MDC where appropriate (examples: ICC = 0.65–0.88; gait-event ICC = 0.94–1.00).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard Error of Measurement (SEM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate of the measurement error in the same units as the measure (e.g., SEM in frames or degrees, SEM = 0.3–1.9 frames; SEM = 1.39°–2.76°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report SEM alongside ICC to indicate precision; use SEM to compute minimal detectable change (MDC) or limits of agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal Detectable Difference / Minimal Detectable Change (MDC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Smallest change that can be interpreted as real beyond measurement error (e.g., MDC with 95% confidence = 2.2–2.3 mm for acromiohumeral distance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute from SEM and report with confidence level; use to interpret clinical significance of change scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity, specificity, and Youden index
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagnostic/screening accuracy metrics for checklists or screening tools (e.g., sensitivity 82.2%, specificity 77.7%, Youden index 0.6 for warning signs checklist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established criterion/reference standards (e.g., ASQ, Gesell) to compute; report values and interpret screening effectiveness for intended setting (community vs clinical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion and concurrent validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a measure correlates with a gold standard or established criterion (e.g., correlations with ASQ, GESELL, or other validated scales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess via correlation coefficients (Pearson, Spearman), agreement statistics, or by comparing predictive relationships; report magnitude and CI and describe criterion used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct, discriminative, and evaluative validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the measure reflects the construct of interest, can discriminate between groups/states, and can detect change over time (evaluative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate statistical tests (correlations, group comparisons, responsiveness analyses); report which validity facets were tested and findings (examples: discriminative and evaluative validity present except for some subscales).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive validity and criterion-related validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which instrument scores predict relevant outcomes (e.g., FoodMATS scores predicting 'Least Healthy' food sales or violence risk judgments predicting community violence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test with regression analyses or event-history analyses, report effect sizes and incremental validity over other models or instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical significance threshold for scale scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition of what constitutes a clinically meaningful change (e.g., a 1-point difference on 5-point photonumeric scales shown to be clinically significant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish via expert review of image pairs or anchor-based methods; report mean absolute differences for clinically different vs not-different pairs with confidence intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-friendliness and feasibility (time, clarity, ease of use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical attributes of a scale such as time required, clarity, and ease of use as judged by users (e.g., RASS found less time consuming, clearer, and easier than alternatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include user surveys or usability assessments as part of validation; report qualitative feedback and relative comparisons between instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale development: assessment guide, verbal descriptors, and exemplar images
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements recommended when creating ordinal photonumeric scales: assessment guide, verbal descriptors, morphed images, and real-subject images for each grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these components to improve rater agreement and to define clinical anchors; validate by testing interrater and intrarater reliability across sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring algorithm rationale and validation
rubrics_metrics.description: When producing composite scores (e.g., FoodMATS), the scoring algorithm should represent the theoretical impact of features and be validated empirically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate algorithm via correlations with external metrics (e.g., sponsorship dollars) and regression models predicting relevant outcomes; report explained variance and statistical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item selection and subscale creation based on theory, expert consensus, and policy relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Group items into subscales using conceptual frameworks grounded in theory and expert input (example: MAPS used theory/expert consensus/policy relevance to create subscales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report item inclusion/exclusion, number of items per subscale, and interrater reliability at tiered levels of aggregation (item, subscale, overall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of number of categories and category definition on agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Granularity of response categories affects reproducibility (e.g., many-category variables had poor specific agreement; binary variables showed better agreement for absence than presence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reducing number of categories or providing rater training to improve agreement; report category-specific agreement and consider collapsing rare categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding, standardized protocol, and study design elements for reliability studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological features required to obtain unbiased reliability estimates (e.g., blinded raters, standardized assessment protocols, separate sessions, appropriate test–retest intervals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe blinding procedures, timing between ratings (examples: 48 hours, ≥2 months, 3 weeks), number of raters, and sample characteristics; use multiple raters and independent ratings when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of statistical tests appropriate to data type
rubrics_metrics.description: Select agreement/statistical tests matching data scale and study design (e.g., kappa for categorical, ICC for continuous, Spearman/Pearson for correlations, t-tests/regression for comparisons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify exact statistic (e.g., ICC model), report p-values and confidence intervals, and when appropriate use multi-rater kappa variants (e.g., Randolph's free-marginal multi rater kappa) or percent agreement as supplement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of measurement precision and variability (CI, SEM, SD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include precision estimates like confidence intervals, SEM, and standard deviations alongside point estimates of reliability and validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report 95% CIs for ICCs/kappas, SEM and MDC values, and descriptive statistics (means and SD) to contextualize reliability findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of expert vs non-expert raters
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether rater expertise affects reliability (examples: expert and non-expert raters showed similar or differing reliability across variables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report subgroup reliability by rater experience and discuss implications for training requirements and generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of gold-standard or reference modality where available
rubrics_metrics.description: When a gold standard exists (e.g., radiographic examination for spine curves), compare the new/noninvasive method against it to evaluate validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use radiographic or other accepted gold standards for criterion validity; if gold standard is impractical, justify and document the reference used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item-level reliability reporting and aggregation tiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Report reliability for individual items and for aggregated subscales/overall scores (examples: MAPS reported item-level reliability then subscale-level reliability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide counts of items with good/excellent/moderate/low reliability and describe how aggregation affects reliability; present tiered results (item → subscale → overall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and education as a modifier of reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision of training or additional clinical interaction can improve rater skills and agreement (e.g., nurses found video education useful but requested additional interaction; suggestion that practical training could improve IETA agreement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include and report any rater training, and consider assessing pre/post training reliability; recommend hands-on or interactive elements where simple video/guide training is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation thresholds for qualitative descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use qualitative language to interpret numeric reliability measures (examples used across studies: 'moderate', 'substantial', 'almost perfect', 'good/excellent').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the numeric ranges used for descriptors (if applied) and be consistent when labeling κ/ICC values to aid interpretation across studies.
